bib.title: Memex(RL): Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agents via Indexed Experience Memory

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Memex(RL): Scaling Long-Horizon LLM Agents via Indexed Experience Memory. Zhenting Wang, Huancheng Chen, Jiayun Wang, Wei Wei (Center for Advanced AI, Accenture). arXiv:2603.04257v1 [cs.CL], 4 Mar 2026. Preprint.

COVERAGE: All 22 pages, 69,636 chars. Pages 1-13 are body, 14-17 references (skimmed; not all read closely), 18-22 are Appendix A (proofs) and B (prompt). Extraction was clean. Figure 2-5 data are images; only their captions and the text describing them were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: MemexRL training lifts task success from 24.22% to 85.61% on the modified ALFWorld, and cuts peak working context by about 43%.
  number: 24.22% -> 85.61%; peak working context 16934.46 -> 9634.47 tokens; ">3.5x" success
  setup: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (MoE, ~3B active), modified ALFWorld, 3553 training tasks, 32K window, 8K penalty threshold. The comparison is the same Memex agent loop with vs without RL, not against another memory method.
  quote: "MemexRL increases the task success rate from 24.22% to 85.61%, while reducing the peak working context length from 16934.46 to 9634.47 tokens. This corresponds to more than a3.5× improvement in task success together with an approximately 43% reduction in peak working context."
  where: p.13 (Sec 5.2); Fig 4 caption p.12
- claim: Training curves: rollout success rises from about 20% to over 90%, and total penalty falls from about -0.4 to about -0.1.
  number: 20% -> >90%; -0.4 -> -0.1
  setup: training rollouts, same run as above. Training success (>90%) is higher than the held-out evaluation figure (85.6%).
  quote: "the rollout task success rate increases from approximately 20% to over 90% during training. At the same time, Figure 3 shows that the total penalty improves from around−0.4to approximately−0.1."
  where: p.12
- claim: RL changed memory behaviour. The agent compresses less (about 6.5 to 3 calls per episode) and reads more (about 1 to 6-7 calls per episode).
  number: Compress 6.5 -> ~3; Read ~1 -> 6-7 per episode
  setup: evaluation set during training, same model and environment
  quote: "the mean number of CompressExperience calls per episode decreases from about 6.5 to about 3, while the mean number ofReadExperience calls increases from about 1 to around 6–7."
  where: p.13 (Fig 5)
- claim: Peak working context after training (9,634) still sits above the 8,000-token penalty threshold, so the budget is only approached, not met.
  number: 9,634 vs 8,000
  quote: "The results show that the peak working context length afterMemexRL training is close to the threshold."
  where: p.13; Fig 4 caption p.12
- claim: Core design. CompressExperience replaces the working context with a short indexed summary (status plus an index map of (index, description) pairs) and archives full content in an external key-value store. ReadExperience(index) dereferences an index exactly and re-injects the content. The system prompt and task are never compressed. Memory operations are tools in the same action space as environment tools.
  number: none
  setup: Definitions 1-2, Algorithm 1
  quote: "M←[𝑚 0,𝑢,IndexedSummary]" and "keep the active reasoning state small, but do not throw evidence away."
  where: pp.5-7
- claim: Indices give exact, auditable lookup, unlike semantic-similarity retrieval over noisy near-duplicate fragments.
  number: none
  quote: "This makes memory access precise and auditable because an index points to a concrete archived artifact rather than to an approximate semantic match."
  where: p.2
- claim: Archiving has two modes. The model either writes the content itself or gives three text anchors (start, mid, end) and the system archives the matching span verbatim. The mid anchor guards against false matches.
  number: none
  quote: "the model specifies three short text anchors (start_anchor, mid_anchor, end_anchor) that uniquely identify a span within the current conversation. The system locates the matching span and archives it verbatim"
  where: p.5
- claim: Reward is task success minus three penalties, each normalised to [0,1] (context overflow, redundant tool calls, malformed calls).
  number: none; formula R = R_task - P_context - P_redundancy - P_format
  setup: context penalty sums max(0, C_t - tau) over steps, divided by tau*T; redundant penalty counts identical (tool, args) calls with no state change in between
  quote: "𝑅=𝑅 task−𝑃 context−𝑃 redundancy−𝑃 format.(1)"
  where: p.8
- claim: Compression timing is learned, not a hard rule. A "[Context Status: working=w, total=t, threshold=L]" line is appended each step and warnings fire near the threshold, so the agent compresses voluntarily. The paper contrasts this with forced compression in Lu et al. 2025.
  number: none
  quote: "This design transforms context management from a system-enforced constraint into a learnable skill."
  where: p.9
- claim: Segmented trajectory processing. The trajectory is split at each compression into k+1 segments, each trained as its own sample with the shared terminal reward. This gives the write policy credit for effects that show up later (GRPO group-relative advantage).
  number: none
  quote: "all segments originating from the same trajectory share the identical terminal reward𝑅, which preserves credit assignment to earlier compression decisions"
  where: p.8-9
- claim: Theory. If the summary is B-bounded decision-sufficient, a Memex policy using at most B reads per step matches the full-context optimal policy. Working context is then bounded by tau_sigma + B*L, so the compression ratio grows without bound as history grows.
  number: bound C_work <= tau_sigma + B*L
  setup: the assumptions are strong, namely that sufficiency holds at every step. The authors say this is a regime characterisation, not a learnability guarantee.
  quote: "Our goal is not to prove thatMemexRL always learns such summaries in practice, but to characterize the regime in which indexed summaries and bounded dereferencing are sufficient"
  where: p.9-10; proofs in App A, pp.18
- claim: The benchmark is deliberately modified so the agent depends on memory. Admissible commands are hidden, the initial room description is stripped, "look" is allowed once per episode, and the summary is truncated to 300 tokens. Object IDs must therefore be stored in db_blocks and read back.
  number: 300 tokens
  quote: "the summary produced byCompressExperienceis truncated to 300 tokens, forcing the agent to store detailed information (e.g., object IDs) in structureddb_blocks"
  where: p.12
- claim: Training details.
  number: lr 5e-6, weight decay 0.1, KL 0.001, batch 32 prompts, GRPO group size 8, 32K context, 8K penalty threshold, truncated importance sampling clip 2.0
  setup: Slime framework, INT4 rollout with QAT backward pass (BF16 gradients). Warm-started from supervised demonstrations of well-formed summaries and blocks before RL.
  quote: "The context window size and the context penalty threshold used in training are 32K and 8K, respectively. The batch size is 32 (i.e., 32 prompts for each rollout step). The group size for GRPO is 8"
  where: p.12; warm start p.9
- claim: Worked compression example (SWE/sympy bug task). Six steps of reasoning and tool output, about 4,000 tokens, collapse into an index summary of about 300 tokens, with indices like ctx_units_code_excerpt_001.
  number: ~300 tokens summary
  quote: "IndexedSummary (approx. 300 tokens):"
  where: p.6 (illustrative, not a measured result)

LIMITS
- Only one model (Qwen3-30B-A3B), one environment (a modified, harder ALFWorld), and one training run. No seeds or variance are reported.
- No baselines against other memory methods. The paper makes no head-to-head comparison with MemGPT, summary-only, ReSum, SUPO, FoldGRPO or AgentFold. The abstract claim of being "less lossy than summary-only approaches" rests on the design argument, not on a measured comparison. Only Memex before and after RL is compared.
- The environment is built so that memory reads are required (look limited to once, summary capped at 300 tokens). The gain is partly an artefact of that design.
- Peak context after training (9.6K) is still above the 8K threshold.
- The theory assumes decision-sufficiency, and the authors concede it does not show RL learns such summaries.
- No test on real software-engineering or web tasks, even though the SWE example is used for illustration. No evaluation of retrieval accuracy, index quality or store growth. The store D is a plain key-value map, so there is no eviction, scaling or cost analysis.
- The abstract and conclusion say "challenging long-horizon tasks" but only ALFWorld is reported.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) and MemoryBank (Zhong et al., 2024), the early memory frameworks. Later memory work: Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025), Memory OS (Kang et al., 2025), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2025).
- RL for memory and summarisation: MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2025b), MemAgent (Yu et al., 2025), Memory-R1 (Yan et al., 2025), Mem-alpha (Wang et al., 2025b), SUPO (Lu et al., 2025), ReSum (Wu et al., 2025), FoldGRPO (Sun et al., 2025), AgentFold (Ye et al., 2025).
- The extended mind (Andy & Chalmers 1998), the hippocampal memory indexing theory (Teyler & DiScenna 1986), ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), GRPO-style updates, and the Slime RL framework (Zhu et al., 2025).

CODE
- Algorithm 1 loop (p.7). Per step: append ContextStatus(M,tau); the agent emits (z_t, c_t). If Compress: write each (index, content) into D and set M <- [m0, u, IndexedSummary]. If Read: o <- D[index] and append it. If Finish: return. Otherwise execute the tool and append the output.
- Status line (p.6): "[Context Status: working tokens=6932, threshold=8000]"
- Tool call format (App B, p.21): {"name": "CompressExperience", "arguments": {"summary": "Index map:\n- ctx_data_001 - ...", "db_blocks": [{"db_index": "ctx_data_001", "db_content": "..."}]}} and {"name": "ReadExperience", "arguments": {"db_index": "ctx_code_001"}}
- Prompt rule worth keeping (p.20): "Strongly recommended when working > 0.8 * threshold"; "When compressing multiple times: include ALL previous indices in your new summary (copy them over), then add new ones."

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): the loop. A long trajectory is replaced by an index summary plus an external store, and ReadExperience(Index I) pulls the content back. It is the clearest picture of the design.
- Fig 2 (p.11): training success rate, about 20% to over 90%.
- Fig 3 (p.11): total penalty, -0.4 to -0.1.
- Fig 4 (p.12): (a) success 24.2% to 85.6%; (b) peak working context 16,934 to 9,634 tokens against the 8,000 threshold.
- Fig 5 (p.13): Compress calls 6.5 to 3; Read calls 1 to 6-7.
(Captions only; I did not run figures.py.)

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Subscript and math symbols are partly garbled in extraction (for example "andchanged" word-joins), but the numbers are intact. The training-time success figure (>90%) and the evaluation figure (85.61%) are different measurements, so do not mix them. The comparison to MemGPT in the target note: Memex adds learned (RL) write/read policy and exact-index recall, whereas the note's MemGPT numbers (32.1% vs 92.5%) come from a different paper and setup. I did not read the target note beyond its first 60 lines.
